claims.statement: packages/shared owns the browser-agnostic data model and reusable logic that both servers and browser extensions depend on, with protocol.ts defining the WebSocket envelope, auth/presence messages, browser capability names, presence metadata, tab-listing shapes, staged upload messages, and download/fetch status shapes; protocol shapes must not be duplicated in servers or adapters.

servers/websocket is the state-light transport and routing layer that authenticates clients with the local pairing token and forwards messages between the MCP server and connected browser extensions; presence is runtime-only and disappears when the socket closes.

servers/mcp is the agent-facing MCP surface exposing browser resources, tools, prompts, and skills, reaching browser extensions via the WebSocket relay; it also ships a demo site under servers/mcp/demo and skill markdown under servers/mcp/skills.

Browser extensions live under clients/extensions/chrome and clients/extensions/safari; Chrome is MV3 with chrome.* namespace and Safari is MV2 with browser.* namespace, text-only badge, and broad host permissions at install time, but both share the same product rules (user-controlled activation, explicit request/response, no streaming, context before content, short-lived ID targeting) and keep shared behavior in @brijio/shared.

Firefox is currently a placeholder only: clients/extensions/firefox contains only a README reserving the client boundary, and Firefox packaging, permissions, and user-control behavior should be designed in a separate ADR before any implementation starts.

Product and business framing lives in README.md, docs/project/POSITIONING.md, and docs/project/CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md, where CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md is the authority for the current product contract and support status and must be updated when capabilities or support status change.

Security and trust docs (docs/security/THREAT_MODEL.md, TRUST_BOUNDARIES.md, SECURITY_GUARANTEES.md) record the trust assumptions behind the bridge and why the project avoids credential export, session cloning, ambient browser surveillance, and continuous streaming.

Design history lives in docs/architecture/decisions/* (numbered ADRs, the authority for architectural decisions) and completed feature/operational explanations in docs/artifacts; ADRs are especially valuable when changing browser actions, protocol shapes, or connection behavior.

The practical cross-domain change order from AGENTS.md is: update the shared protocol or an ADR first, then the WebSocket relay and/or MCP server, then the browser adapters; for protocol or browser-capability changes check the full path shared protocol -> WebSocket relay -> MCP surface -> shared controller -> Chrome adapter -> Safari adapter -> integration tests, and consider both Chrome and Safari.

Browser actions must preserve explicit per-call browser and tabId targeting with no hidden selected-browser or selected-tab session state; when tabId is optional the documented active-tab fallback applies unless an accepted ADR changes it, and page context must be re-read after navigation or a mutation that can invalidate short-lived target IDs.
